explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says they sell "the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals." A pair of sandals is not much, and that's the whole point. Somebody who needed help got treated like he was worth less than a pair of shoes.

A cloak does come up later in the passage, sort of. The LORD talks about garments taken in pledge (Amos 2:8). But here in verse 6, the needy are sold "for a pair of sandals." Sandals, friend, not even a whole outfit.

A belt is a fun guess, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says they sell "the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals." I think the sandals make the charge sting even more, because it's such a small price.
Yes, baker. The LORD says a man and his father have relations with the same girl "and so profane My holy name." That's heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. The LORD says it touches His holy name.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says a man and his father have relations with the same girl "and so profane My holy name." It's a heavy part of the passage, and I think we should treat it that way. The text doesn't water it down, so neither will I.
That's right. In the house of their God, they drink wine "obtained through fines." Picture it: wine paid for by money squeezed out of people. I'd be nervous taking a sip of that.
Offerings sound like they'd fit the house of God, I'll give you that. But the verse says the wine was "obtained through fines." Nobody gave that wine freely, friend.
Trade sounds so fair and friendly, doesn't it? That's not what the LORD says. He says the wine was "obtained through fines," so it came from penalties, not a good deal.

Not quite, baker. The LORD says, "it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them." The Amorite was tall like cedars and strong as oaks, so Israel's men weren't the secret ingredient here. The LORD was.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them," and the Amorite was "like that of the cedars." Israel didn't win by being bigger. He did it, from the fruit above to the roots below.
Yes, Egypt. The LORD says, "I brought you up from the land of Egypt." He's reminding Israel of what He did for them. That's quite a list of reminders, and it's only getting started.
Babylon is a sneaky guess, but it's not the one here. The LORD says, "I brought you up from the land of Egypt." Egypt is the land He is pointing back to.
Assyria's a good guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "I brought you up from the land of Egypt." He's pointing to where they started, not to a place on a later map.

Forty is right. The LORD says He "led you forty years in the wilderness." He led them the whole way, and the goal was that they might take possession of the land of the Amorite. Forty years is a long road, baker.
Seventy is a number that shows up in other places in the Bible, but not here. The LORD says He "led you forty years in the wilderness." It's forty, and He was the one leading.
Twelve is a good Bible number, I'll give you that. Not this time, though. The LORD says He "led you forty years in the wilderness." Forty years of Him leading the way.
Close, but no, baker. The LORD says they "commanded the prophets not to prophesy." So the prophets weren't free to keep going. They were told to hush.

That's right. The LORD says, "you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy." The prophets were the ones He raised up, and Israel told them to stop. They told them to hush.
Yes, their escape. The LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift." So even the fast ones can't outrun it. Racing away is the one move they were counting on.
Weapons are a smart guess, friend, but they're not what the verse says. The LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift." The thing that fails is their getting away.
Horses do come up in the next verse, with the horseman (Amos 2:15). But for the swift in verse 14, the LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift." Their getting away is what fails.
Oh, I wish I could say yes, baker. But the LORD says, "the horseman will not save his life." Not even a horseman gets a pass. Nobody gets to say they had a ride out.
Right. The LORD says, "the horseman will not save his life." Even with a horse under him, he doesn't make it out. Speed doesn't help him at all.
That's it, baker. The LORD says, "Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day." Even the bravest one runs, with nothing on him. That's how far the mighty fall.
Caves are a fine guess, but the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, "Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day." They run, and they run with nothing.
That's the opposite, friend. The LORD says the archer "will not stand his ground" (Amos 2:15), and even the bravest "will flee naked on that day." Nobody holds the line.
